title: Basic definitions and concepts
text:
I would like this section to contain the fundamentals of representation theory of finite groups. As an undergraduate at UVA, I made the mistake of not taking Algebra 2, the second course in the graduate algebra sequence that dealt with representation theory and field theory. These posts are meant to provide a somewhat detailed account of my self-study process to make up for that.
In each of these entries I plan to state key theorems and propositions and their proofs (most of the time), as well as some examples and exposition to illustrate those statements. So, without further ado, let’s get into what representation theory is.
In abstract algebra, one of the core objects we study are groups. They can be studied in the abstract of course, but one of the most fundamental ways that we study these objects is through their actions. We can examine actions just simply on sets, but we can glean more information if we study how they act on other algebraic objects, such as vector spaces. This is the general philosophy of finite group representation theory: we study how groups act as symmetries of a vector space. Sometimes these vector spaces have additional structure, like an inner product, and in these cases even more can be said. We will revisit this richer situation later, but for now let’s understand some basic definitions.
Recall that by \(GL(V)\) we mean the group of linear automorphisms of \(V\). Fixing a basis \(\beta=\{e_1,...,e_n\}\), we can identify \(V\) with \(\k^n\) and thus \(GL(V)\) with \(GL_n(\k)\), sending \(f \in GL(V)\) to \([f]_{\beta}\), its matrix representation.

Definition 1 (Representation of a group \(G\)) Let \(G\) be a group and \(V\) a vector space over a field \(\k\). A representation of \(G\) on \(V\) is a group homomorphism \[
    \rho: G \lrarrow GL(V)
\]
If we have a basis \(\beta\) as above, we obtain an n-dimensional represenation of \(G\): \[
    \rho: G\lrarrow GL_n(\k)
\]

While these definition look similar, they are not the same, as a representation \(\rho: G \lrarrow GL_n(\k)\) can be identified with \(\rho: G \lrarrow GL(V)\) where \(V=\k^n\), but the converse is not true. This basically boils down to the fact that the inverse map isn’t well-defined due to the fact that we have to choose a basis. This means that two representations for the same vector space can differ by conjugation of a change of basis matrix:
\[
    \rho_{\beta'}=T^{-1}\rho_{\beta} T
\] where \(T\) is the change of basis matrix from the basis \(\b\) to \(\b'\). Therefore, we should consider representations up to a different notion of equivalence rather than strictly equal. This is formalized in the following definition:

Definition 2 Two matrix representaitons \(\r_1,\r_2:G\lrarrow GL_n(\k)\) are equivalent if there exists a \(T \in GL_n(\k)\) such that \(\r_2= T^{-1} \r_1 T\)
Similarly, two representations \(\r_1,r_2:G \lrarrow GL(V)\) are equivalent if there exists a \(T\in GL(V)\) such that \(\r_2= T^{-1} \r_1 T\)
It’s clear that these notions are equivalence relations, and we now have a bijection on the level of equivalence classes of matrix and linear representations.
There are countless examples of representations that can be found anywhere really, but here I will focus on one important one. Let \(G=SL_2(\k)\), the group of \(2\times 2\) invertible matrices over \(\k\) with determinant \(1\). Now there is an obvious representation \[
\r:G \lrarrow GL_2(\k)
\] acting as the inclusion homomorphism, but we will soon show that \(G\) has a representation in every dimension \(n\).

title: Chapter 1: Basic definitions and two big theorems
text:
From what I can tell, the motivating problem for the development of the tools discussed in the Orange Book is trying to understand the structure of \(\pi_*^S\), the stable homotopy groups of spheres. If we look at it like a ring, we can’t describe it in terms of generators and relations, particularly because all elements in degree \(\geq 1\) are nilpotent due to a theorem of Nishida. Thus, we have to view \(\pi_*^S\) from a different perspective. Despite each element having finite order, we can identify certain infinite families of elements in the stable stems, which we will touch on later. These infinite families are called periodic, and with this new point of view, we’d like to know whether all elements of the stable stems are a part of some periodic family, which would indeed give us a great deal of information about the global structure of stable homotopy groups.
There are two main theorems in this book: the nilpotence theorem and the periodicity theorem. The latter is more geared toward this global structure of homotopy groups as just discussed, and the former theorem implicates a certain (co)homology theory \(MU\), complex bordism theory, which will become central to studying the homotopy category of CW complexes/spectra. In this post I will document the necessary terms and definitions to be able to state these two results, while trying to weave in some sort of narrative to clarify things for myself. For now I will keep things (as the book does for the first few chapters) in terms of spaces, then transition to spectra. Perhaps I will revise this to make everything consistent, but we’ll see.

title: Chapter 1: Basic definitions and two big theorems
text:
Nilpotence theorem
We begin with a definition.

Definition 1 Suppose we have a map \(f:\Sigma^d X \xrightarrow{f} X\), where \(d\geq 0\). We may iterate it (appropriately suspending) by considering the composites \[
\cdots \Sigma^{3d} X \xrightarrow{\Sigma^{2d}f} \Sigma^{2d} X \xrightarrow{\Sigma^d f} \Sigma^d X \xrightarrow{f} X
\] We denote these composites by \(f,f^2,f^3\), etc. For such a self-map \(f\), we say that it is nilpotent if some suspension of \(f^t\) for some \(t>0\) is nullhomotopic. Otherwise, \(f\) is periodic.

Recall that a homology theory \(E\) is a functor from the homotopy category of based spaces to the category of graded abelian groups. By functoriality, we always have the unique homomorphism \[
E_*(X)\xrightarrow{\epsilon} E_*(\text{pt})
\] Taking the kernel of this map gives us the reduced homology of \(X\), denoted by \(\overline{E}_*(X)\). For ordinary homology, this is simply removing a \(G\) summand of \(H_0(X;G)\).
Coming back to the above definition, by functoriality of homology theories and the suspension isomorphism, if we have a reduced homology theory \(\overline{E}_*\) and apply it to the map \(f\), we will obtain an endomorphism of \(\overline{E}_*(X)\) raising the grading by \(d\). We may now state the nilpotence theorem.

Theorem 1 Nilpotence theorem. There is a homology theory \(MU_*\) such that a self-map \(f\) of a finite CW complex is stably nilpotent if and only if some iterate of \(\overline{MU}_*(f)\) is trivial.

Essentially, nilpotence is detected by the homology theory \(MU_*\). Compared to ordinary homology, \(MU_*\) is quite interesting. For one, it takes values in the category of modules over a certain graded ring \(L\), called the Lazard ring, which is isomorphic to \(MU_*(\text{pt})\). Additionally, these modules also have an interesting action by a certain group \(\Gamma\), adding even more algebraic structure to the picture. We will discuss this homology theory and these other algebraic gadgets in more depth later.

title: Chapter 1: Basic definitions and two big theorems
text:
Periodicity Theorem
We now pivot to the periodicity theorem and its setup. We will employ the use of another extraordinary homology theory called Morava K-theory, but first we need to discuss localization at the prime \(p\).
Let’s take the ring \(\ZZ\) and consider the set \(S\coloneqq \ZZ/(p)\), the elements of \(\ZZ\) that lie outside of the prime ideal \((p)\) (i.e. \(S\) consists of all integers not divisible by \(p\)). Now, consider the set \[
\ZZ_{(p)}\coloneqq \{\frac{a}{b} : a\in\ZZ, b\in S \}
\]
This is in fact a ring, with the property that it has a unique maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}=p\ZZ_{(p)}\). Such a ring is called a local ring. Now, if we want to apply this to a \(\ZZ\)-module \(M\), we keep \(S\) the same, and we again let \(M_{(p)}\) consist of formal fractions in \(M\) with denominators in \(S\). However, we declare two fractions \(\frac{m_1}{s_1},\frac{m_2}{s_2}\) to be equal if there exists an element \(t\in M\) such that \(t(s_2m_1-s_1m_2)=0\) in \(M\). The reason for this equivalence relation is to account for the torsion of \(M\). Another, much more straightforward of constructing \(M_{(p)}\) is to simply tensor it with \(\ZZ_{(p)}\). In practice this is what we will mean when we discuss localization in the future, just tensor everything with \(\ZZ_{(p)}\) and proceed.
We now return to homotopy. One can perform an analogous procedure for spaces, but it is a little technical so I won’t go through the construction here. The point is, for any CW complex \(X\), there is a unique \(X_{(p)}\) such that for any homology theory \(E_*\), we have \(\overline{E}_*(X_{(p)})\cong \overline{E}_*(X)\otimes \ZZ_{(p)}\). As one would expect, \(X_{(p)}\) is called the \(p\)-localization of \(X\), and if \(X\) is finite, we say \(X_{(p)}\) is a \(p\)-local finite complex. Some key properties of this construction are listed below.

Proposition 1 Suppose \(X\) is a simply-connected CW complex such that \(\overline{H}_*(X)\) consists entirely of torsion.

If this torsion is prime to \(p\), then \(X_{(p)}\) is contractible.
If it is all \(p\)-torsion, then \(X\) is \(p\)-local, i.e., \(X_{(p)}\) is equivalent to \(X\).
In general \(X\) is homotopy equivalent to the wedge sum of its \(p\)-localizations for all the primes \(p\) in this torsion.


From the definition of \(p\)-localization, we have the following chain of equalities/isomorphisms for a finite simply-connected CW complex \(X\): \[
\overline{H}_*(X)\cong \bigoplus_p(\overline{H}_*(X)\otimes \ZZp) = \bigoplus_p \overline{H}_*(X_{(p)})=\overline{H}_* \bigl( \bigvee_p X_{(p)}\bigr)
\]
For Whitehead’s theorem to apply, we need a map that carries this isomorphism of reduced homology to obtain a homotopy equivalence, and fortunately we do have such a map coming from the natural map that arises out of localization from \(X\) to \(X_{(p)}\).
Now, if we consider the smash product \(\overline{H}_*(X \wedge Y)\) the Künneth formula tells us this is isomorphic to \(\overline{H}_*(X)\otimes \overline{H}_*(Y)\). If \(X=X_{(p)}\) and \(Y=X_{(q)}\) for distinct primes \(p,q\), then this tensor product will clearly be trivial and thus so will \(X_{(p)}\wedge X_{(q)}\). Furthermore, this implies that the cartesian product of two coprime localizations is the same as their wedge sum.
The reason we introduced the concept of \(p\)-localizations and \(p\)-local spaces is due to the fact that we can form many interesting self-maps using these spaces. However, in this case \(MU_*\) is not the homology theory that we will utilize. Instead, we will use Morava K-theory. Its basic properties are as follows:

Proposition 2 For each prime \(p\) there is a sequence of homology theories \(K(n)_*\) for \(n\geq 0\) with the following properties:

\(K(0)_*(X)=H_*(X;\QQ)\) and \(\overline{K(0)}_*(X)=0\) when \(\overline{H}_*(X)\) is all torsion.
\(K(1)_*(X)\) is one of \(p-1\) isomorphic summands of mod \(p\) complex K-theory.
\(K(0)_*(\text{pt})=\QQ\) and for \(n>0\), \(K(n)_*(\pt)=\ZZ/p [v_n,v_n^{-1}]\), where \(|v_n|=2(p^n-1)\). It turns out that this ring is a graded field in the sense that every module over it is free. Furthermore, \(K(n)_*(X)\) is a \(K(n)_*(\pt)\)-module.
There is a Künneth isomorphism \[
K(n)_*(X\times Y)\cong K(n)_*(X)\otimes_{K(n)_*(\pt)} K(n)_*(Y)
\]
Let \(X\) be a \(p\)-local finite CW complex. If \(\overline{K(n)}_*(X)\) vanishes, then so does \(\overline{K(n-1)}_*(X)\).
If \(X\) is as above, then \[
\overline{K(n)}_*(X)=K(n)_*(\pt)\otimes \overline{H}_*(X;\ZZ/p)
\]

for \(n\) sufficiently large. In other words, \(\overline{K(n)}_*(X)\) is nontrivial if \(X\) is simply connected and not contractible.

We need one last definition to state the periodicity theorem.

Definition 2 A \(p\)-local finite complex \(X\) has type \(n\) if \(n\) is the smallest integer such that \(K(n)_*(X)\) is nontrivial. If \(X\) is contractible, then \(X\) has type \(\infty\).


Theorem 2 Periodicity theorem. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be \(p\)-local finite CW complexes of type \(n\) where \(n<\infty\).

There is a self map \(f:\Sig^{d+i}\longrightarrow \Sig^i X\) for some \(i\geq 0\) such that \(K(n)_*(f)\) is an isomorphism and \(K(m)_*(f)\) is trivial for \(m>n\). We will call such a map \(f\) a \(v_n\)-map. When \(n=0\) then \(d=0\). When \(n>0\), \(d\) is a multiple of \(2(p^n-1)\).
Suppose \(h:X\longrightarrow\) is a continuous map and assume both spaces have been suspended sufficiently to be the target of a \(v_n\)-map. Let \(g:\Sig^e Y \longrightarrow Y\) be a self-map as above. Then there are positive integers \(i\) and \(j\) with \(di=ej\) such that the following diagram commutes up to homotopy.






Moreover, \(i\) and \(j\) can be chosen independently of \(h\).

As we can see, if we want to understand periodic self-maps, we better understand Morava K-theories. We note that it isn’t logically necessary for \(X\) to have type \(n\), but it just happens to be the only interesting case. (If the type of \(X\) is larger than \(n\), then the trivial map satisfies the theorem. If the type is smaller than \(n\), then for \(d=0\) the degree \(p\) map satisfies the theorem, and if \(d>0\), the theorem follows as \(K(m)_*(f)=K(m)_*(\pt)\otimes H_*(f)\) and some iterate of \(H_*(f)\) must be trivial reasons due to the finiteness of \(X\)). From 2. we see that \(f\) is actually unique in the sense that if we have some other periodic self-map \(g\) and take \(Y=X\) and \(h\) the identity, it shows that \(f^i\simeq g^j\) for some \(i,j\).
Thus we have stated the two main theorems of this book. Already, things are getting complicated as we are dealing with extraordinary homology theories, and there is a lot of math that we have glossed over. In the next few posts I’ll be discussing \(MU_*\) and \(K(n)_*\) in more depth. There are some very cool connections with algebra and number theory that will drive the discussion and are necessary to develop the theory.

title: Some Stable Homotopy Groups of \(\mathbb{RP}^2\)
text:
In this post I’d like to post a solution to exerices 12.1 from Mosher and Tangora’s Cohomology Operations and Applications in Homotopy Theory. This problem took me a lot of time to work out, but I think it’s important to know how to do, so I’ve decided to make a post about it.
I should mention before starting that whenever \(\pi_i^S(-)\) appears, I mean the 2-component of the stable homotopy group. Additionally, much of the notation and terminology used here is from Mosher and Tangora’s book, but I’ll try and indicate when I’m using something specific from there. Also, I will denote the stable homotopy groups of spheres by \(\pi_*^S\) for brevity.
The problem:

Let \(M_n=S^n \cup_{2} e^{n+1}\). We can also think of this as \(\S^{n-1}\RP^2\), the \((n-1)\)-suspension of the real projective plane. Compute the homotopy groups \(\pi_{n+k}(M_n)\) for large \(n\) and small \(k\).

So there are two methods that I will pursue here: one is using the induced homotopy long exact sequence coming from the cofiber sequence \[
S^n\lrarrow S^n \lrarrow M_n
\] where the first arrow is the degree 2 map, and the second will be using the Serre spectral sequence in the style of chapter 12 of Mosher and Tangora’s book.
Let’s begin with the cofiber sequence. Now, since \(\pi_*^S\) is a generalized homology theory, the cofiber sequence above induces a long exact sequence in stable homotopy groups:





examining the bottom portion of this long exact sequence, we have \[
\pi_2^S \xrightarrow{\cdot 2} \pi_2^S \to \pi_2^S(M_n) \to \pi_1^S \xrightarrow{\cdot 2} \pi_1^S
\]
As we can see, \(\pi^S_0(M_n)\) is the cokernel of the degree 2 map on \(\pi_0^S(S^n) \cong \ZZ\), which is \(\ZZ/2\), and so \(\pi^S_0(M_n) \cong \ZZ/2\). Now, since multiplication by 2 is injective on \(\pi_1^S\cong \ZZ\), we know that the map \(\pi_1^S(M_n) \to \pi_0^S\) is the zero map, and thus \(\pi_1^S(M_n)\) is isomorphic to the cokernel of the degree 2 map on \(\pi_1^S\). However, since \(\pi_1^S \cong \ZZ/2\), this map is the zero map, and thus \(\pi_1^S(M_n) \cong \ZZ/2\) as well.
Moving to the 2nd stable stem, this is where things start to get interesting. Examining the relevant portion of the long exact sequence and substituting known values, we have \[
\ZZ/2 \xrightarrow{\cdot 2} \ZZ/2 \to \pi_2^S(M_n) \to \ZZ/2 \xrightarrow{\cdot 2} \ZZ/2
\]
Since multiplication by 2 is the zero map on \(\ZZ/2\), this exact sequence reduces to a short exact sequence \[
0 \to \ZZ/2 \to \pi_2^S(M_n) \to \ZZ /2 \to 0
\]
meaning that up to an extension problem, \(\pi_2^S(M_n)\) is isomorphic to \(\ZZ/2 \oplus \ZZ/2\). To figure out if the extension is trivial or not, we will use the Serre spectral sequence, which is the second method I mentioned at the beginning.

title: Chapter 2: Homotopy groups and the chromatic filtration
text:
This chapter introduces us to the “chromatic picture” of homotopy groups/theory. As I said in the beginning of the Chapter 1 post, the graded ring \(\pi_*^S\) is not well-described using generators and relations. (The graded ring structure coming from the composition product which works because we are working stably.) There’s been many results on specific elements and families of elements, for example we know all elements are nilpotent and that that all stable homotopy groups of positive degree are finite, but the global structure is still a mystery. However, there are recognizable patterns within the infinite families, and using this structure, we can indeed understand the global picture. This will be put into more precise language, but I think this is the main idea.
Besides looking at things from this new perspective, in this post we’ll also develop our understanding of the aforementioned infinite families and how they come about. First we’ll need some setup though.

title: Chapter 2: Homotopy groups and the chromatic filtration
text:
Setup
First, a definition.

Definition 1 A cofiber sequence is a sequence of spaces and maps of the form \[
X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{i} C_f \xrightarrow{j} \Sigma X \xrightarrow{\Sigma f} \cdots
\]
where each space to the right of \(Y\) is the mapping cone of the map preceeding the map to it, and each map to the right of \(f\) is the canonical inclusion of a maps target into its mapping cone.

Using this sequence, we obtain three fundamental long exact sequences in homotopy.

Proposition 1 Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be path-connected CW complexes.

For any space \(Z\), the cofiber sequence above induces a long exact sequence \[
[X,Z] \xleftarrow{f^*} [Y,Z] \xleftarrow{i^*} [C_f,Z] \xleftarrow{j^*} [\Sig X, Z] \xleftarrow{\Sig f} \cdots
\]

Everything to the left of \([C_f,Z]\) is naturally a group and so exactness means the usual thing. The terms to the right don’t have an intrinsic group structure, but we can make exactness make sense since each of these sets contains a distinguished element (the trivial map). 2. Let \(E_*\) be a homology theory. Then there is a long exact sequence \[
\cdots \xrightarrow{j_*} \overline{E}_m(X) \xrightarrow{f_*} \overline{E}_m(Y) \xrightarrow{i_*} \overline{E}_m(C_f) \xrightarrow{j_*} \overline{E}_{m-1}(\Sig X) \xrightarrow{f_*} \cdots
\]

Suppose \(X\) and \(Y\) are each \((k-1)\)-connected and let \(W\) be a finite complex which is a double suspension with top cell in dimension less than \(2k-1\). Then there is a long exact sequence of abelian groups \[
[W,X] \xrightarrow{f_*} [W,Y] \xrightarrow{i_*} [W,C_f] \xrightarrow{j_*} [W,\Sig X] \xrightarrow{\Sig f} \cdots
\]

This sequence will terminate at the point where the connectivity of the target exceeds the dimension of \(W\).

I’ll note that the assumptions that we see in the above proposition are in place are due to the restrictions of the homotopy category of spaces. If we were working over spectra instead, we’d get long exact sequences of abelian groups that extend infinitely in both directions for (1) and (3).
From these induced long exact sequences (LES), we have the following corollary.

Corollary 1 Suppose \(X\) is a \(p\)-local finite CW complex of type \(n\) for \(n\) finite. Then, the cofiber of the \(v_n\) self-map from the periodicity theorem has type \(n+1\).


Proof. We first assume \(X\) has been sufficienty suspended to be the target of a \(v_n\) map \(f\), and we let \(W\) be the cofiber. Using Proposition 1, we consider the following LES: \[
\cdots \overset{j_*}{\longrightarrow} \overline{K(m)}_t(\Sigma^d X) \overset{f_*}{\longrightarrow} \overline{K(m)}_t(X) \overset{i_*}{\longrightarrow} \overline{K(m)}_t(W) \overset{j_*}{\longrightarrow} \overline{K(m)}_{t-1}(\Sigma^d X) \overset{f_*}{\longrightarrow} \cdots
\]
For \(W\) to be type \(n+1\), we must show that \(K(m)_*(W)=0\) for \(m<n+1\) and that \(f\) induces an isomorphism on \(K(n+1)_*(W)\). If \(m<n\), then since \(X\) is type \(n\), we know that \(\overline{K(m)}_*(X)=0\) and thus also \(\overline{K(m)}_*(\Sig^d X)=0\), forcing \(\overline{K(m)}_*(W)=0\). For \(m=n\), we know that \(f_*\) is an isomorphism for every \(t\) as \(X\) is type \(n\), and thus by exactness \(\overline{K(n)}_*(W)=0\). When \(m>n\), \(f_*=0\) by definition, and we also have that \(\overline{K(m)}+_*(X)\neq 0\) by the contrapositive of (5) of the properties of Morava K-theory. Now, if \(f_*=0\), then by exactness, \(j_*\) must be a surjection and \(i_*\) an injection and so as a \(K(m)_*\)-module, \(\overline{K(m)}_t(W)\) is an extension of \(\overline{K(m)}_t(\Sig^{d+1} X)\) by \(\overline{K(m)}_t(X)\). However as all \(K(m)_*\)-modules are free, this exact sequence splits and we have \[
\overline{K(m)}_*(W)\cong \overline{K(m)}_*(\Sigma^{d+1} X) \oplus \overline{K(m)}_*(X)
\]
Therefore, \(W\) has type \(n+1\).

Periodic maps: examples and general procedure
Now we will focus on periodic maps and how they can give us nontrivial elements of \(\pi_*^S\). First we will look at some foundational examples and then move into the generalized framework.

Example 1  

The degree map \(p:S^1 \rightarrow S^1\) where \(S^1\subset\CC\) given by \(z \mapsto z^p\) is periodic in the sense that none of its iterates are nullhomotopic. All of its suspensions are essential as well.
Let \(V(0)_k\) (aka mod \(p\) Moore space) be the cofiber of the degree \(p\) map on \(S^k\). It has been shown by Adams and Toda that for sufficiently large \(k\), there is a periodic map \[
\Sigma^q V(0)_k \xrightarrow{\alpha} V(0)_k
\]

where \(q=8\) for \(p=2\) and \(q=2p-2\) for \(p\) odd. In the context of the periodicity theorem, \(n=1\). The induced map on \(K(1)_*(V(0)_k)\) is multiplication by \(v_1\) for \(p\) odd and \(v_1^4\) for \(p=2\). The \(p=2\) case is interesting and what’s even more interesting is that there is no self-map inducing multiplication by a smaller power of \(v_1\) (for reasons which I don’t completely understand at the moment). 3. Suppose \(p\geq 5\) and take the cofiber of the map \(\alpha\) above and denote it by \(V(1)_k\). It has been shown that for \(k\) sufficiently large, there is a periodic map \[
\Sigma^{2p^2-2} V(1)_k \xrightarrow{\beta} V(1)_k
\] inducing multiplication by \(v_2\) in \(K(2)\)-theory. 4. For \(p\geq 7\), denote by \(V(2)_k\) the cofiber of the map \(\beta\) above. There is a periodic map \[
\Sigma^{2p^3-2} V(2)_k \xrightarrow{\gamma} V(2)_k
\]

title: Chapter 3: MU and formal group laws
text:
In Chapter 2, we saw a new perspective on understanding the homotopy groups \(\pi_*(Y)\) of a CW complex via the chromatic filtration. This reformulation depends (in a way that I don’t totally understand) on the nilpotence and periodicity theorems of Chapter 1. To my understanding, the goal of this chapter is to mirror this structure/way of thinking algebraically.
In algebraic topology, this is usually formalized by a functor \(F:\FH\rightarrow \mathbf{Alg}\), where \(\FH\) represents the category of finite CW complexes and homotopy classes of maps between them, and \(\mathbf{Alg}\) is some “algebraic” category, just meaning a space of algebraic objects that we can make sense of in the usual fashion. This category will be denoted henceforth by \(\CG\), and it will mean the category of modules over a certain ring \(L\) equipped with an action of a certain group \(\Gamma\) that is compatible with a natural action of \(\Gamma\) on \(L\). The functor \(F\) will be the homology theory \(MU_*\), complex bordism.
Studying this algebraic category reveals a very organized structure in the theory of these special \(L\)-modules, which is analogous to things we saw with Morava K-theory and the periodicity theorem in chapter 1. We will take this analogy further by defining a notion of type for these modules, which will allow us to state in more precise terms this correspondence due to \(MU_*\).

title: Chapter 3: MU and formal group laws
text:
Complex bordism
Given two smooth, closed, \(n\)-dimensional manifolds \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) and maps \(f_i:M_i\rightarrow X\), where \(X\) is some space, we say \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are bordant if there exists a map \(f:W\rightarrow X\) for \(W\) an \((n+1)\)-dimensional manifold such that \(\partial W=M_1\sqcup M_2\) and \(f\) restricted to \(\partial W\) is the disjoint union of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\). The groups \(MU_n(X)\) are defined to be the \(n\)-dimensional bordism classes under the operation of disjoint union, where we require all manifolds to satisfy certain nice conditions (all manifolds are required to be stably complex, but defining this isn’t really important for us). We will denote by \(MU_n\) the group \(MU_n(\pt)\). Under the operation of cartesian product, the graded group \(MU_*\) inherits the structure of a graded ring, which we denote by \(MU_*\).
Due to a result of Milnor, as a graded ring, \(MU_*\) is isomorphic to the polynomial ring
\[
\ZZ[x_1,x_2,...]
\]
where \(|x_i|=2i\).
There is a natural action of \(MU_*\) on \(MU_*(X)\) described as follows: given \(x\in MU_*(X)\) represented by a map \(f:M\rightarrow X\), and an element \(\lambda\in MU_*\) represented by a manifold \(N\), \(\lambda x\) is represented by the composite \[
M\times N\rightarrow M\xrightarrow{f} X
\]
Now, \(MU_*\) is a homology theory as I mentioned above (I won’t prove it), and thus by Brown representability corresponds to a spectrum, which we denote by \(MU\). Just as for any other spectrum, we can also associate to \(MU\) a cohomology theory \(MU^*\). For conventional reasons, the graded rings \(MU_*(\pt)\) and \(MU^*(\pt)\) are isomorphic to each other except with the gradings reversed, so that \(MU^*=MU^*(\pt)\) is a polynomial ring over \(\ZZ\) with a generators \(x_i\) of degree \(-2i\). Additionally, the cohomology theory \(MU^*\) comes equipped with a cup product, and combining this with the \(MU^*\)-module structure of \(MU^*(X)\), \(MU^*(X)\) is upgraded to an \(MU^*\)-algebra. The cohomology theory \(MU^*\) also has a Künneth-type isomorphism \[
MU^*(X\times Y)\cong MU^*(X)\otimes_{MU^*} MU^*(Y)
\]
but this isomorphism doesn’t occur in general, as there have to be certain assumptions in place on the spaces \(X\) and \(Y\) and the \(MU^*\)-module structure of \(MU^*(X)\) and \(MU^*(Y)\). However, for what we will consider we won’t have to worry about these assumptions.
It’s thus very natural to study modules over the ring \(MU_*\) to understand this homology theory. Something that’s quite interesting is that we can define this ring completely algebraically as well. To do this we will need to make some definitions regarding formal group laws.

title: Chapter 3: MU and formal group laws
text:
Formal group laws

Definition 1 Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. A formal group law (FGL) over \(R\) is a formal power series \(F(x,y)\) in \(R\) such that the following are satisfied 1. \(F(x,0)=F(0,x)=x\) (identity) 2. \(F(x,y)=F(y,x)\) (commutativity) 3. \(F(x,F(y,z))=F(F(x,y),z)\) (associativity)

FGLs are invertible; the inverse of \(F(x,y)\) is the FGL \(i(x)\) such that \(F(x,i(x))=0\)


Additive FGL: \(F(x,y)=x+y\). Its inverse is \(i(x)=-x\).
Multiplicative FGL: \(F(x,y)=x+y+xy=(1+x)(1-y)-1\). Its inverse is \(i(x)=\frac{-x}{1+x}\).


There is a universal FGL \(G(x,y)\), over a ring \(L\) called the Lazard ring such that for any FGL over \(R\) \(F\) the coefficients of \(F\) are captured in a unique ring homomorphism \(\theta:L\rightarrow R\). More explicitly, the universal FGL has the form \(G(x,y)=\sum_{i,j} a_{i,j}x^i y^j\) where \(a_{i,j}\in L\), and if \(\theta:L\rightarrow R\) is the corresponding ring homomorphism to \(F\), we can write \(F\) uniquely as \[
F(x,y)=\sum_{i,j} \theta(a_{i,j}) x^iy^j
\]
Lazard proved that as a ring, \(L\) is isomorphic to \(\Z[x_1,x_2,\cdots]\). If we put a grading on \(L\) such that the coefficients \(a_{i,j}\) of the universal FGL \(G\) have degree \(2(1-i-j)\), then the degree of the generator \(x_i\) is \(-2i\), which is clearly isomorphic to \(MU^*\). In fact, this isomorphism is actually deeper than algebra. Let’s make this precise. We will consider the space \(X=\CC P^{\infty}\), which is the classifying space of complex line bundles. Due to this fact, there is a map \[
f:\CC P^{\infty} \times \CC P^{\infty} \rightarrow \CC P^{\infty}
\]
which induces the tensor product of line bundles. It is a fact that \(MU^*(X)\cong MU^*[[x]]\), where \(|x|=2\), so taking the induced map \(MU^*(f)\) we get a map
\[
MU^*(\CC P^{\infty}\times \CC P^{\infty})\xleftarrow{f^*} MU^*(\CC P^{\infty})
\]
that is determined by where the 2-dimensional generator \(x\) is sent. Utilizing the Künneth-type isomorphism above, we have an isomorphism \[
MU^*(\CC P^{\infty}\times \CC P^{\infty})\cong MU^*[[x\otimes 1,1\otimes x]]
\]
so that our map \(f^*\) really corresponds to a power series \(F(x\otimes 1,1\otimes x)\). This power series \(F\) can be shown to be a formal group law, and thus must correspond to a homomorphism \(\theta:L\rightarrow MU^*\). Quillen proved that this map is in fact an isomorphism. This means that the FGL associated to complex cobordism is the universal one (the “co” prefix is used because we are discussing the cohomology theory \(MU^*\)). Thus, if we just move reverse the gradings, we may consider \(MU_*(X)\) to be an \(L\)-module.

title: Chapter 3: MU and formal group laws
text:
Deeper into the algebra
We are thus compelled to study the structure of the category \({}_L\mathbf{Mod}\) of \(L\) modules. However, we can actually refine our objects of interest to the subcategory \(\CG\) of \(L\)-modules equipped with an action of the group \(\Gamma\) that is compatible with the action of \(\Gamma\) on \(L\).
Let \(\Gamma\) be the group of power series over \(\ZZ\) of the form \[
\gamma=x+b_1x^2+b_2x^3+\cdots
\]
where the group operation is functional composition. The natural action of \(\Gamma\) on \(L\) is defined as follows: let \(G(x,y)\) be the universal FGL over \(L\) and let \(\gamma\in \Gamma\). Then \(\gamma^{-1}(G(\gamma(x),\gamma(y)))\) is another FGL over \(L\) and is therefore induced by an endomorphism \(L\rightarrow L\). By definition, \(\gamma\) is invertible so that this endomorphism is an automorphism, and thus we have the desired action. There is also an action of \(\Gamma\) on \(MU_*(X)\), but defining this is quite technical and isn’t necessary.
It may seem a bit random to narrow our focus to the category \(\CG\), but the group \(\Gamma\) comes from topology and its action is therefore a natural thing to take into account. Recall that in ordinary cohomology, \(H^*(X)\) (mod 2 coefficients suppressed) is module over the Steenrod algebra. This action massively restricts the types of algebraic modules that can arise out of real topological spaces. The group \(\Gamma\) is playing an analogous role specifically to the multiplicative operations. Multiplicative operations in \(MU\)-theory are much more complicated than in ordinary cohomology, but their behavior is dictated by where they send the generator \(x\in MU^2(\CC P^{\infty})\), and \(\Gamma\) captures this behavior. Not only does studying \(\CG\) get rid of topologically impossible \(L\)-modules, but the \(\Gamma\)-action clears up the picture immensely. To explicitly elaborate on this we need a few more definitions from FGL theory.

Definition 2 For each integer \(n\), the \(n\)-series \([n](x)\) is given by the recursive formula \[\begin{align}
[1](x) &=x \\
[n](x) &=F(x,[n-1](x)) \qquad n>1\\
[-n](x)&= i([n](x))
\end{align}
\]

These \(n\)-series depend on the integer \(n\) and the FGL \(F\). They satisfy \[\begin{align}
[n](x) & =nx \mod(x^2)\\
[m+n](x) & = F([m](x),[n](x))\\
[mn](x) & = [m]([n](x))
\end{align}
\]
For example, if \(F\) is the additive FGL, \([n](x)=nx\) and if \(F\) is the multiplicative FGL, \([n](x)=(1+x)^n-1\). Of particular interest are the \(p\)-series. Operating in characteristic \(p\), the leading term is always \(ax^q\) where \(q=p^h\). We make the following definition.

Definition 3 Let \(F(x,y)\) be a FGL over a ring \(R\) in which the prime number \(p\) is not a unit. If the \(\mod p\) reduction of \([p](x)\) has the form \[
[p](x)=ax^{p^h} + \text{higher terms}
\]
with \(a\) invertible, then we say that \(F\) has height \(h\) at \(p\). If \([p](x)=0 \mod p\), then the height is infinity.

From the above examples, the height of the additive FGL is infinity since \([p](x)=px=0\mod p\). For the multiplicative FGL, its height is 1 since \([p](x)=x^p \mod p\). This leads to a very important result for the theory of FGLs.

Theorem 1 Classification of FGLs. Two FGLs over the algebraic closure of \(\FF_p\) are isomorphic if and only if they have the same height.

Let \(v_n\in L\) denote the coefficient of \(x^{p^n}\) in the \(p\)-series for the universal FGL (prime \(p\) is omitted from the notation). It can be shown (but won’t be done here) that \(v_n\) is indecomposable in \(L\) so that \(v_n\) is a polynomial generator in dimension \(2p^n-2\). Let \(I_{p,n}\subset L\) denote the prime ideal \((p,v_1,...,v_{n-1})\).
Now I can make concrete my earlier remark about the structure of \(\CG\) being a bit more organized. :::{#thm-invariant-ideal} Invariant prime ideal theorem.
The only prime ideals in \(L\) which are invariant under the action of \(\Gamma\) are \(I_{p,n}\) as just defined, where \(p\) is a prime integer and \(n\) is a nonnegative integer, possibly \(\infty\).
Moreover, in \(L/I_{p,n}\), for \(n>0\), the subgroup fixed by \(\Gamma\) is \(\ZZ/p[v_n]\). In \(L\) itself, the invariant subgroup is \(\Z\). :::
\(L\) is very complicated as a ring—it’s generated by a countably infinite amount of variables, but when we look at it in the context of the \(\Gamma\)-action, we see that this action is very rigid. Using this theorem, we can understand the modules in \(\CG\). First, recall that for a Noetherian ring \(R\), any finitely generated \(R\)-module \(M\) admits a finite filtration \[
0=F_0M\subset F_1 M\subset F_2M\subset \cdots \subset F_k M=M
\]
where the subquotients \(F_iM/F_{i-1}M\) are isomorphic to \(R/I_i\) for a prime ideal \(I_i\). Now \(L\) is not Noetherian, but it is the direct limit of Noetherian rings, so this finite filtration property is still satisfied (for reasons I don’t understand). For modules in \(\CG\), we may actually choose the filtrations and prime ideals such that they are all \(\Gamma\)-invariant. Stated more formally: :::{#thm-landweber-filtration} Landweber filtration theorem. Every module \(M\) in \(\CG\) admits a finite filtration by submodules in \(\CG\) as above such that each subquotient is isomorphic to a suspension (the modules are graded) of \(L/I_{p,n}\) for some prime \(p\) and some finite \(n\). :::
So not only do we only need to focus on the prime ideals \(I_{p,n}\) as opposed to all of them, but additionally the other generators of \(L\) that are not \(v_n=x_{p^n-1}\) for some \(n\) act freely on any module in \(\CG\), since they are never affected by any of the quotients \(L/I_{p,n}\). Furthermore, Ravenel notes that in practice people don’t care about these other generators either. After localizing at a prime \(p\), instead of \(MU\)-theory, people opt for \(BP\)-theory, Brown-Peterson theory. The coefficient ring for this theory is what we would expect: \[
V_p=\ZZp[v_1,v_2,...]
\]
which is the result of tensoring away the frivolous generators. In another post I’ll discuss this more, given its prevalence in modern research, but it seems quite complicated at the moment, and since the book operates with \(MU\)-theory so will I.
Using these theorems, we can prove some results that similar to results in chapter 1. :::{#cor} Suppose \(M\) is a \(p\)-local module in \(\CG\) (i.e. \(M\otimes \ZZp\cong M\)) and \(x\in M\). 1. If \(x\) is annihilated by some power of \(v_n\), then it is annihilated by some power of \(v_{n-1}\). In other words, if \(v_n^{-1} M=0\) (each element in \(M\) is annihilated by some power of \(v_n\)), then \(v_{n-1}^{-1} M=0\). ::: This statement is analogous to the statement about Morava K-theory, where we saw that if \(\overline{K(n)}_*(X)=0\), then \(\overline{K(n-1)}_*(X)=0\) if \(X\) is \(p\)-local and finite.

Proof. For the second part of 1., we know \(M\) has a finite filtration with subquotients isomorphic to a suspension of \(L/I_{p,m}\). If \(m\leq n\), then \(v_n\notin I_{p,m}\) and so \(v_n\) will act freely on \(M\), contradicting oour assumption that \(v_n^{-1}M=0\). Thus, all \(m\) must be greater or equal to \(n+1\). In each of these layers, \(v_{n-1}\in I_{p,m}\) and so if \(x\in M\), say \(x\in F_k M\), then \(v_{n-1} x=0\) in \(F_k/F_{k-1}M\) and so \(v_{n-1}\in F_{k-1}M\). One then repeats this procedure \(k-1\) more times and since the filtration is finite, this will terminate and thus \(v_{n-1}^{-1} M=0\).



If \(x\neq 0\), then there is an \(n\) such that \(v_n^k x\neq 0\) for any \(k\). So, if \(M\) is nontrivial, then so is \(v_n^{-1}\) for any sufficiently large \(n\).


This statement is analogous to the isomorphism \(\overline{K(n)}_*(X)\cong K(n)_*\otimes \overline{H}_*(X;\ZZ/p)\) for a \(p\)-local finite complex \(X\). Ravenel asserts that the functor \(v_n^{-1}\overline{MU}_*(X)_{(p)}\) is a homology theory that vanishes on a finite \(p\)-local CW complex if and only if \(\overline{K(n)}_*(X)\) and that you could replace one with the other in the statement of the periodicity theorem.

If \(v_{n-1}^{-1}M=0\) then there exists a positive integer \(k\) such that multiplication by \(v_n^k\) in \(M\) commutes with action of \(\Gamma\).
Conversely, if \(v_{n-1}^{-1}M=0\) is nontrivial, then there is no positive integer \(k\) such that multiplication by \(v_n^k\) in \(M\) commutes with the action of \(\Gamma\) on \(x\).

title: Chapter 3: MU and formal group laws
text:
This chapter discusses the extraordinary (co)homology theory \(MU\), also known as complex (co)bordism and the algebra of its cohomology. Geometrically, \(MU\) tells us about bordism classes of manifolds with certain nice properties, but this information isn’t really necessary to our discussion. Indeed, what is more important is the algebra that arises from it. After a brief introduction and definition of \(MU\), we will move on to the other central subject of this chapter: formal group laws (FGLs). These objects live entirely in the realm of algebra, but are intimately connected with \(MU\), so we’ll spend some time with them.
In the last post we developed a new way of looking at \(\pi_*^S(Y)\) by filtering it chromatically, where at each step we focus on \(v_n\)-torsion or periodic behavior (with \(v_0=p\)). In a certain sense, \(MU\) paired with an infinite group \(\Gamma\) allow us to mirror this chromatic behavior algebraically using the theory of FLGs.

title: Chapter 3: MU and formal group laws
text:
\(MU\)-theory
Given two smooth, closed, \(n\)-dimensional manifolds \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) and maps \(f_i:M_i\rightarrow X\), where \(X\) is some space, we say \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are bordant if there exists a map \(f:W\rightarrow X\) for \(W\) an \((n+1)\)-dimensional manifold such that \(\partial W=M_1\sqcup M_2\) and \(f\) restricted to \(\partial W\) is the disjoint union of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\). Under the operation of disjoint union, we obtain the \(n^\text{th}\) bordism groups of \(X\).
Embedding a manifold \(M\) into Euclidean space allows us to define its normal bundle, and if we take the dimension of our Euclidean space to be large enough, this normal bundle is unique in a certain sense. This is called the stable normal bundle. Manifolds that admit a complex linear structure on their stable normal bundle are called stably complex.

\(MU_n(X)\) is the \(n^\text{th}\) complex bordism group of \(X\). It is the bordism group of \(X\) requiring all manifolds to be stably complex.

As mentioned earlier, this group and other bordism groups in general are interesting geometrically in their own right (i.e. the Pontryagin-Thom isomorphism), but we won’t delve into this much. We are much more interested in the algebra that arises from this construction. The case where \(X\) is a point is of much interest. These groups are simply bordism classes of stably complex manifolds, and we can actually endow \(MU_*(\text{pt})\) with the structure of a graded ring under the Cartesian product. We will denote this group by \(MU_*\) for simplicity. Due to Milnor, we can write down explicitly what this ring looks like:

The complex bordism ring \(MU_*\) is isomorphic to \[
\ZZ[x_1,x_2,\cdots]
\] where the dimension of the generator \(x_i\) is \(2i\).

The generators \(x_i\) don’t have an easy description as manifolds, but Ravenel notes that complex projective space \(\CC P^i\) serve as generators of \(MU_*\otimes \QQ\).
Before transitioning to our discussion of FGLs, we note that as a graded group, \(MU_*(X)\) is a module over the coefficient ring \(MU_*\). To see this, if we are given \(x\in MU_*(X)\) and \(f:M\rightarrow X\), and \(\lambda\in MU_*\) is represented by the manifold \(N\), then \(\lambda x\) is reppresented by the composite \[
M\times N\rightarrow M\xrightarrow{f} X
\]

title: Chapter 3: MU and formal group laws
text:
Formal group laws

Definition 1 A formal group law (FGL) over a commutative ring \(R\) is a formal power series \(F(x,y)\) over \(R\) that satisfies the following three conditions: 1. \(F(x,0)=F(0,x)=x\) (identity) 2. \(F(x,y)=F(y,x)\) (commutativity) 3. \(F(x,F(y,z))=F(F(x,y),z)\) (associativity)

FGLs are invertible; the inverse of \(F(x,y)\) is the FGL \(i(x)\) such that \(F(x,i(x))=0\)


Additive FGL: \(F(x,y)=x+y\). Its inverse is \(i(x)=-x\).
Multiplicative FGL: \(F(x,y)=x+y+xy=(1+x)(1-y)-1\). Its inverse is \(i(x)=\frac{-x}{1+x}\).


A nice property of FGLs is that there is a universal one over a certain ring \(L\), called the Lazard ring, named after the person who proved this. This means that any FGL over \(R\) is completely determined by a unique ring homomorphism \(\theta:L\rightarrow R\). Explicitly, if we write our universal FGL as \(G(x,y)=\sum_{i,j} a_{i,j}x^i y^j\) where \(a_{i,j}\in L\), then for any FGL \(F(x,y)\) over \(R\), there is a unique ring homomorphism \(\theta:L\rightarrow R\) that encodes the coefficients of \(F\): \[
F(x,y)=\sum_{i,j} \theta(a_{i,j}) x^iy^j
\]
Another result due to Lazard is that \(L\) is isomorphic to the polynomial algebra \(\Z[x_1,x_2,\cdots]\), and that if we put a grading on \(L\) such that \(a_{i,j}\) has degree \(2(1-i-j)\), then \(|x_i|=-2i\), which looks awfully familiar to the form of the coefficient ring \(MU_*\), just with the grading reversed. There is actually a cohomology theory \(MU^*\) associated to \(MU_*\) similar to the case of ordinary homology and cohomology. The coefficient ring of \(MU^*\) is isomorphic to \(MU_*\) but with the gradings reversed, so obviously \(MU^*\cong L\) as graded rings. What’s interesting is that this isomorphism comes from topology, i.e. it’s not simply because the rings have the same algebraic structure. Briefly, \(MU^*(X)\) has a cup product so that it’s an algebra over \(MU^*\). Considering \(X=\CC P^{\infty}\), which is the classifying space for complex line bundles, so we have a map \(f:\CC P^{\infty} \times \CC P^{\infty} \rightarrow \CC P^{\infty}\) which corresponds to the tensor product. Looking at \(MU^*(f)\), we have a map \[
MU^*(\CC P^{\infty}\times \CC P^{\infty})\xleftarrow{f^*} MU^*(\CC P^{\infty})
\]
which is determined by where it sends the generator \(x\) of \(MU^*(X)\cong MU^*[[x]]\). Now there is a natural isomorphism (analogous to the Künneth formula) \(MU^*(\CC P^{\infty}\times \CC P^{\infty})\cong MU^*[[x\otimes 1,1\otimes x]]\), and thus the map \(f^*\) determines a power series \(F(x\otimes 1, 1\otimes x)\) which can be shown to be a FGL. By Lazard’s universality theorem above, this power series must correspond to a ring homomorphism \(\theta: L\rightarrow MU^*\). This was proven to be an isomorphism by Quillen, thus the universal FGL is in fact the FGL associated to complex cobordism (we say “co”bordism here just because we are talking about the “co”homology theory \(MU^*\)). All of this goes to show that the theory of formal group laws is intimately connected with complex (co)bordism and we will investigate this relationship further.

title: Chapter 3: MU and formal group laws
text:
More algebraic structure
As a functor, we’ve seen that \(MU_*\) takes values in the category of \(L\)-modules (by ignoring the reversal of the grading). However, we can actually restrict the latter category to a smaller subcategory with additional structure coming from the action of a certain group \(\Gamma\). This is the group of power series over \(\ZZ\) having the form \[
\gamma=x+b_1x^2+b_2^x^3+\cdots
\]
where the group operation is composition. We define an action of \(\Gamma\) on \(L\) as follows. Let \(G(x,y)\) be the universal FGL over \(L\) and let \(\gamma\in \Gamma\). Then \(\gamma^{-1}(G(\gamma(x),\gamma(y)))\) is another FGL over \(L\) and is therefore induced by an endomorphism \(L\rightarrow L\). By definition, \(\gamma\) is invertible so that this endomorphism is an automorphism, and thus we have the desired action. There is also an action of \(\Gamma\) on \(MU_*(X)\) which is compatible with the action of \(\Gamma\) on \(MU_*\). Explicitly, given \(x\in MU_*(X)\), \(\gamma\in \Gamma\), and \(\lambda\in L\), we have \(\gamma(\lambda x)=\gamma(\lambda) \gamma(x)\). The details of how this is constructed are technical and not super important for this discussion.
If we denote by \(\FH\) the category of finite CW complexes and homotopy classes of maps between them and by \(\CG\) the category of finitely presented graded \(L\)-modules equipped with an action of \(\Gamma\) that is compatible with its action on \(L\), we may regard \(\overline{MU}_*\) as a functor from \(\FH\rightarrow \CG\). We are thus motivated to study the category \(\CG\). To do so we need more information regarding the algebra of FGLs and \(L\)-modules equipped with the aforementioned \(\Gamma\)-action.

Definition 2 For each integer \(n\), the \(n\)-series \([n](x)\) is given by the recursive formula \[\begin{align}
[1](x) &=x \\
[n](x) &=F(x,[n-1](x)) \qquad n>1\\
[-n](x)&= i([n](x))
\end{align}
\]

These \(n\)-series depend on the integer \(n\) and the FGL \(F\). They satisfy \[\begin{align}
[n](x) & =nx \mod(x^2)\\
[m+n](x) & = F([m](x),[n](x))\\
[mn](x) & = [m]([n](x))
\end{align}
\]
For example, if \(F\) is the additive FGL, \([n](x)=nx\) and if \(F\) is the multiplicative FGL, \([n](x)=(1+x)^n-1\). Of particular interest are the \(p\)-series. Operating in characteristic \(p\), the leading term is always \(ax^q\) where \(q=p^h\). We make the following definition.

Definition 3 Let \(F(x,y)\) be a FGL over a ring \(R\) in which the prime number \(p\) is not a unit. If the \(\mod p\) reduction of \([p](x)\) has the form \[
[p](x)=ax^{p^h} + \text{higher terms}
\]
with \(a\) invertible, then we say that \(F\) has height \(h\) at \(p\). If \([p](x)=0 \mod p\), then the height is infinity.

From the above examples, the height of the additive FGL is infinity since \([p](x)=px=0\mod p\). For the multiplicative FGL, its height is 1 since \([p](x)=x^p \mod p\). This leads to a very important result for the theory of FGLs.

Theorem 1 Classification of FGLs. Two FGLs over the algebraic closure of \(\FF_p\) are isomorphic if and only if they have the same height.

Let \(v_n\in L\) denote the coefficient of \(x^{p^n}\) in the \(p\)-series for the universal FGL (prime \(p\) is omitted from the notation). It can be shown (but won’t be done here) that \(v_n\) is indecomposable in \(L\) so that \(v_n\) is a polynomial generator in dimension \(2p^n-2\). Let \(I_{p,n}\subset L\) denote the prime ideal \((p,v_1,...,v_{n-1})\). The following theorem tells us that these prime ideals are the only ones we need to concern ourselves with.

Theorem 2 Invariant prime ideal theorem.
The only prime ideals in \(L\) which are invariant under the action of \(\Gamma\) are \(I_{p,n}\) as just defined, where \(p\) is a prime integer and \(n\) is a nonnegative integer, possibly \(\infty\).
Moreover, in \(L/I_{p,n}\), for \(n>0\), the subgroup fixed by \(\Gamma\) is \(\ZZ/p[v_n]\). In \(L\) itself, the invariant subgroup is \(\Z\).

This theorem places restrictions on the structure of modules in \(\CG\), which is made concrete in the next theorem. Before stating it, we need to recall a few facts from commutative algebra. Recall that finitely generated modules over a Noetherian ring \(R\) have a finite filtration \[
0=F_0M\subset F_1 M\subset F_2M\subset \cdots \subset F_k M=M
\]
in which each subquotient \(F_i M/F_{i-1} M\cong R/I_i\) for some prime ideal \(I_i\subset R\). Now \(L\) is not Noetherian but it is a polynomial ring generated by countably infinite generators, meaning it is a direct limit of Noetherian rings. For reasons I don’t fully understand, finitely presented modules over it admit similar filtrations. For a module in \(\CG\), the submodules and therefore the prime ideals, can be chosen so that they are all invariant under the action of \(\Gamma\). This is summarized in the following theorem.

Theorem 3 Landweber filtration theorem. Every module \(M\) in \(\CG\) admits a finite filtration by submodules in \(\CG\) as above such that each subquotient is isomorphic to a suspension (the modules are graded) of \(L/I_{p,n}\) for some prime \(p\) and some finite \(n\).

These two results are saying that in the context of \(\CG\) (and after localizing at a prime \(p\)), the only generators of \(L\) or \(MU_*\) that are doing anything interesting are the \(v_n=x_{p^n-1}\). The other generators aren’t touched by the quotient \(L/I_{p,n}\) and thus will remain free polynomial variables. This suggests that it might be useful to just tensor away the unwanted variables and instead study the theory of \(L\)-modules with a \(\Gamma\)-action by the corresponding theory of modules over the ring \[
V_p=\ZZp[v_1,v_2,...]
\]
also known as the coefficient ring \(BP_*\) of Brown-Peterson theory. This is the usual method used in chromatic homotopy theory as, according to Ravenel it has algebraic, topological, and computational benefits. However this all comes at the cost of high technicality due to there not being an analog of the group \(\Gamma\).
The following are consequences of the Landweber filtration theorem and resemble some earlier results about Morava K-theory, which isn’t surprising given the same notation for \(v_n\) as important objects.

Suppose \(M\) is a \(p\)-local module in \(\CG\) (i.e. \(M\otimes \ZZp\cong M\)) and \(x\in M\). 1. If \(x\) is annihilated by some power of \(v_n\), then it is annihilated by some power of \(v_{n-1}\). In other words, if \(v_n^{-1} M=0\) (each element in \(M\) is annihilated by some power of \(v_n\)), then \(v_{n-1}^{-1} M=0\). 2. If \(x\neq 0\), then there is an \(n\) such that \(v_n^k x\neq 0\) for any \(k\). So, if \(M\) is nontrivial, then so is \(v_n^{-1}\) for any sufficiently large \(n\). 3. If \(v_{n-1}^{-1}M=0\) then there exists a positive integer \(k\) such that multiplication by \(v_n^k\) in \(M\) commutes with action of \(\Gamma\). 4. Conversely, if \(v_{n-1}^{-1}M=0\) is nontrivial, then there is no positive integer \(k\) such that multiplication by \(v_n^k\) in \(M\) commutes with the action of \(\Gamma\) on \(x\).
